concepts.name: Finite State Machine (FSM)
concepts.definition: A model where an object is always in exactly one of a set of named states and moves between them through defined transitions when conditions are met. NICo uses FSMs to drive each managed host through its lifecycle.

concepts.name: Managed Host
concepts.definition: NICo's record of a physical server together with its DPUs and BMCs, which NICo discovers, prepares, assigns to tenants and cleans up.

concepts.name: Managed Host Lifecycle
concepts.definition: The main sequence of top-level states a managed host goes through: DPU discovery, DPU initialization, host initialization, Ready, Assigned to an instance, and cleanup. There are side paths for validation, reprovisioning, measuring, failure and decommissioning.

concepts.name: NICo Core
concepts.definition: The central NICo service. It persists managed-host state in a database and runs the state-machine handlers, and it can run as several replicas.

concepts.name: Site Explorer
concepts.definition: The NICo component that finds BMC endpoints on the site network and creates managed hosts from what it finds. It also chooses settings such as whether DPF is used.

concepts.name: Scout
concepts.definition: The NICo agent that runs on the host. It reports hardware inventory and discovery data to Core and carries out tasks such as NIC firmware dispatch.

concepts.name: Data Processing Unit (DPU)
concepts.definition: A programmable network card with its own processor and OS (NVIDIA BlueField). NICo uses it to enforce tenant networking for the host. A DPU can also run in plain NIC mode.

concepts.name: BFB (BlueField Bootstream)
concepts.definition: The image format used to install the operating system and firmware on a BlueField DPU. NICo installs a BFB during DPU initialization, during reprovisioning, and a vanilla preingestion BFB during decommissioning.

concepts.name: DOCA Platform Framework (DPF)
concepts.definition: An NVIDIA framework for provisioning DPUs. When Site Explorer selects it, NICo provisions DPUs through DPF instead of its own BFB install path.

concepts.name: Rshim
concepts.definition: A management interface to a BlueField DPU used for things like pushing boot images and reaching the console. NICo enables it during DPU discovery.

concepts.name: Secure Boot
concepts.definition: A firmware feature that only lets signed boot software run. NICo checks it on DPUs and enables or disables it depending on whether BFB install is supported.

concepts.name: Baseboard Management Controller (BMC)
concepts.definition: A separate management chip on a server or DPU. It allows remote power control, firmware configuration and monitoring regardless of the host OS.

concepts.name: Redfish API
concepts.definition: A standard REST API that BMCs expose for remote server management. NICo uses it through libredfish for BIOS settings, boot order, power and firmware jobs.

concepts.name: IPMI over LAN
concepts.definition: An older remote management protocol for BMCs that works over the network. NICo enables it during host initialization.

concepts.name: UEFI/BIOS Configuration
concepts.definition: Applying firmware settings and a UEFI password to a host through the BMC. Some vendors (such as Dell) apply them as scheduled BIOS jobs that need a reboot; NICo polls until setup is confirmed.

concepts.name: Boot Order
concepts.definition: The firmware's ordered list of devices to boot from. NICo sets it so the host boots through the DPU or network as needed.

concepts.name: Host Lockdown
concepts.definition: A mode that blocks changes to the host's BMC and firmware settings from the host side. NICo turns it off to make changes and turns it back on before tenant use.

concepts.name: PXE / iPXE Boot
concepts.definition: Booting a machine over the network. NICo PXE-boots hosts into a discovery image, and tenants can ask for a custom iPXE boot.

concepts.name: Measured Boot Attestation
concepts.definition: An optional check in which the host reports boot measurements and NICo compares them with a trusted bundle of golden values before the host moves on.

concepts.name: SKU and BOM Validation
concepts.definition: A check that compares a host's discovered hardware inventory with an assigned SKU (expected Bill of Materials). The host waits if no SKU is assigned or if the hardware does not match.

concepts.name: Machine Validation
concepts.definition: Test runs on a host, done in a context such as Discovery or Cleanup. A host can skip them by configuration or fail them.

concepts.name: Instance
concepts.definition: A tenant's use of a managed host. Assigning an instance moves the host from Ready to Assigned, and deleting it starts cleanup.

concepts.name: Network Segment and VPC
concepts.definition: Tenant network constructs that the DPUs configure for an instance. Segments must be ready before provisioning can continue.

concepts.name: Network Configuration Version Acknowledgement
concepts.definition: DPU agents report which version of the desired network configuration they have applied. NICo waits until the reported versions match the desired versions before moving on.

concepts.name: Health Reports and Alerts
concepts.definition: Health reports from agents and from overrides are combined into an aggregate. Alert classifications in it, such as PreventHostStateChanges, block state transitions. Host Replace reports take precedence over DPU reports.

concepts.name: BGP Peering with Top-of-Rack Switch
concepts.definition: The DPU's BGP session to the rack's switch on its uplink port (p0). A p0 transport failure blocks the PXE restart.

concepts.name: Live Network Update
concepts.definition: Changing an assigned instance's networking without restarting the host. NICo keeps the old resources until every DPU acknowledges the new configuration and health is clear, then releases them in one transaction.

concepts.name: Host Reprovision
concepts.definition: Updating host firmware through the BMC, either by uploading images or by running scripts, followed by a reset and verification. It can run from Ready or Assigned.

concepts.name: DPU Reprovision
concepts.definition: Reinstalling or updating the DPU OS/firmware (BFB) and then waiting for the network config before rebooting the host. It returns to where it came from.

concepts.name: WaitingForCleanup (Deprovision Cleanup)
concepts.definition: The cleanup after an instance is released. It wipes host storage, including a secure erase and recreation of a BOSS boot volume where present, and then goes back through BOM and machine validation in the Cleanup context.

concepts.name: BOSS Controller
concepts.definition: A Dell boot-drive controller. NICo securely erases it and recreates its volume during cleanup.

concepts.name: DHCP
concepts.definition: The protocol that assigns IP addresses to network interfaces, including out-of-band management and BMC interfaces.

concepts.name: Out-of-Band (OOB) Interface
concepts.definition: A management network interface that is separate from the data network.

concepts.name: Decommissioning
concepts.definition: The terminal path from Ready. It resets host and DPU configuration, suppresses DHCP for the host's MACs, factory-resets the BMCs, and deletes per-device credentials.

concepts.name: Failed State and Failure Causes
concepts.definition: A state recording why a host failed, such as BIOS setup, discovery, measurement or validation failures. Some causes recover automatically once the condition clears, others need an admin.

concepts.name: Managed-Host Reset
concepts.definition: An admin-requested reset that deletes the instance and re-ingests the host. It is the supported way to recover a parked NIC firmware failure.

concepts.name: Force Deletion
concepts.definition: Admin removal of a failed host from NICo. It is refused while NIC firmware work or dispatch obligations are unsettled.

concepts.name: Disable Onboard NICs (Vera Rubin)
concepts.definition: A HostInit step only for Vera Rubin hosts with managed DPUs. It enables and then disables the onboard NICs through the BMC, with persisted 10-second waits between the writes.

concepts.name: NIC Firmware Recovery Engine
concepts.definition: An unreleased, disabled-by-default part of the state machine. It checks non-DPU NIC firmware against a baseline during initial preparation and deprovision, and admits and tracks firmware changes so they can be recovered safely.

concepts.name: NIC Firmware Baseline Policy
concepts.definition: The target firmware chosen per card, machine or site, in that order of precedence. A change only proceeds if the platform (sys_vendor/product_name) and the card (PN/PSID) exactly match the allow-list.

concepts.name: NIC Firmware Admission
concepts.definition: Moving a queued NIC check (Pending) into an admitted operation. Admission freezes the targets, artifacts and lockdown policies and reserves an update slot for the host. Without valid evidence and capacity, the check stays Pending.

concepts.name: NIC Firmware Execution Phases
concepts.definition: The steps an admitted operation goes through for each card: observe the supervisor, unlock, flash, then activate by reboot or card reset. It then checks a fresh inventory and restores the original lockdown policies.

concepts.name: Firmware Supervisor and Receipt
concepts.definition: The local daemon that performs firmware work, plus the receipt Core saves that records which work it accepted and the results. Core uses receipts to resume after restarts without repeating writes.

concepts.name: NIC Readiness Qualification and Restoration Obligations
concepts.definition: Persisted flags saying a NIC card must be restored to baseline or re-qualified through host preparation before allocation. They survive reset and admission being disabled.

concepts.name: Tracked Dispatch
concepts.definition: A record (UUID token and origin) that each participating sender writes before sending a power, DPA or MLX command. An unresolved dispatch blocks further progress until the command's effects are proven settled.

concepts.name: Operator Reconciliation
concepts.definition: The manual procedure used when evidence is uncertain. The operator fences all original senders, preserves the evidence, confirms that tools and hardware have settled, and then conditionally records settlement for the exact token.

concepts.name: Managed-Machine Update Scheduling Budget
concepts.definition: A shared limit on how many hosts can do firmware updates at once. If both limits are unset, capacity is zero and changed NIC work stays pending.

concepts.name: Managed Artifact Cache
concepts.definition: Storage for firmware artifacts. Admitted operations pin their artifacts by digest so they are not evicted during use.

concepts.name: SuperNIC Lockdown and IKM Keys
concepts.definition: A NIC feature that locks firmware changes behind a key. Changing a locked card requires its MAC and its settled current IKM key version.

concepts.name: PN/PSID
concepts.definition: The part number and Parameter-Set ID that identify an NVIDIA NIC model and its firmware configuration. They are used to match cards to the allow-list.

concepts.name: DMI Platform Identity
concepts.definition: The system vendor and product name that the host firmware reports. NIC firmware policy uses them to identify the platform.

concepts.name: DPA (Data Path Accelerator)
concepts.definition: A NIC subsystem with its own agents and firmware policies. Legacy DPA firmware paths must not overlap with the generic NIC firmware engine.

concepts.name: MLX Configuration
concepts.definition: NVIDIA/Mellanox tools and settings for configuring and flashing NIC firmware. Tracked MLX writes create restoration obligations.

concepts.name: Clock Synchronization
concepts.definition: Keeping system clocks in agreement across machines. Core compares Scout collection times with database times and does not correct for skew, so the clocks must be synchronized.

concepts.name: State History and Manual Intervention Alerts
concepts.definition: Diagnostic tools for stuck hosts. State history shows past transitions and errors, and alerts fire when the controller needs an operator to step in.

prerequisites.why: The lifecycle is described as an FSM with states and transitions
The lifecycle is the lifecycle of a managed host
A managed host consists of a server plus its DPUs
Managed hosts are discovered and controlled through their BMCs
Site Explorer creates managed hosts
Redfish is the API that BMCs expose
IPMI is a BMC management protocol
BFB is the DPU OS image
DPF provisions DPUs
Rshim is a DPU management interface
BIOS settings and jobs are applied through the BMC's Redfish API
Boot order is a firmware setting
Lockdown restricts BMC and firmware changes
Both deal with trust in boot software
BOM validation compares the inventory that Scout reports
DPU agents send the version acknowledgements
The configuration being acknowledged is tenant networking
Old resources are released only after DPUs acknowledge the new configuration
Blocking health alerts hold the release of old resources
It updates an assigned instance's network
p0 failures show up as health probe classifications
Network boot relies on DHCP
Firmware is uploaded and tracked through BMC tasks
DPU reprovisioning installs a BFB
Cleanup erases and recreates BOSS volumes
Cleanup continues into validation in the Cleanup context
Decommissioning suppresses DHCP and waits for acknowledgements
The OOB DHCP wait checks the OOB interface MACs
Decommissioning starts from Ready
Recovery goes back into specific lifecycle states
Force deletion is entered from Failed
Its entry points hook into HostInit/Discovered and WaitingForCleanup
Core runs and persists the engine and its admission settings
Cards are matched to the allow-list by PN/PSID
Platforms are matched by sys_vendor/product_name
Admission resolves and freezes the baseline targets
Changed work needs an available update slot
Admission needs fresh inventory and capability flags from Scout
The phases belong to an admitted operation
Each phase observes and depends on supervisor receipts
The Unlocking and RestoringLockdown phases operate on card lockdown
Inventory freshness checks compare timestamps from different hosts

prerequisites.concept: NIC Readiness Qualification and Restoration Obligations
prerequisites.why: Restoration returns cards to the current baseline
Dispatch tracking exists to protect NIC firmware participation
DPA requests are among the tracked senders
MLX writes are tracked senders
Reconciliation settles unresolved dispatch tokens
Unfinished supervisor work requires explicit reconciliation
